tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

# 2026-09-24 — Shared data tier for DuckDB files and API pulls (not done; plan)

## What this is

Eric asked whether the datasets that live on the Mac (the DuckDB files, the other database files,
and the raw API pulls behind them) should move to Supabase so the Windows machine can reach them
and they are backed up in the cloud. This handoff records the decision and the checklist. **Nothing
below has been executed.** It was written from a cloud session that could see only the thin `DEV`
router repo, not the project repos, so every project-specific item must be re-verified on a machine
that has the repos on disk.

## Decision

- **No Supabase.** The files are DuckDB; Supabase is Postgres. Moving them means migrating every
  table, rewriting every pipeline to talk to Postgres over the network, and paying latency on every
  query. The two Supabase projects that already exist (`vald-explorer`, `bookvault`) are both paused
  as INACTIVE, which is what the free tier does after a week idle. That is a preview of how a pipeline
  run a few times a week would go.
- **Raw pulls are the source of truth, not the `.duckdb` files.** Pulls land on the primary storage
  drive (Google Drive) as Parquet or CSV, date-partitioned. Each machine rebuilds its own local
  `.duckdb` from them. The `.duckdb` file is a build artifact and never syncs.
- **DuckDB never opens a file that sits in a Drive-synced folder.** DuckDB and SQLite write in place
  and hold locks. Drive copying a file mid-write corrupts it or spawns "conflicted copy" duplicates.
- **Backup is Drive versioning** (30 days of file versions) plus the existing `dailybackup` Drive
  tier. No new backup system.
- **MotherDuck, not Supabase, if a hosted database is ever wanted.** It is DuckDB in the cloud
  (`ATTACH 'md:'`), no schema migration, no pipeline rewrite. External service, so only for datasets
  with no athlete-identifiable data. Not needed for the two-machine problem.
- **Supabase earns its place only for serving**: a Streamlit dashboard or coach PWA that must read
  live data from a server, or concurrent access by other staff. Separate decision.

## What is wrong with the current setup

1. **Windows live-syncs DuckDB files through Google Drive.** Drive for Desktop backs up all of
   `Desktop\DEV` on Windows. The 09-22 handoff already names the long-term fix as not done: move
   non-regenerable data to `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive` and stop backing up DEV. Any
   `.duckdb` or `.db` a pipeline writes inside DEV on Windows is being copied while it is open.
   The Mac side is safer (the `dailybackup` launchd job is an rsync on a schedule) but can still
   catch a file mid-write.
2. **No cross-machine data root.** Both machines already have a `_DRIVE` link inside DEV pointing at

# 2026-09-24 — Shared data tier for DuckDB files and API pulls (not done; plan)

## What this is

Eric asked whether the datasets that live on the Mac (the DuckDB files, the other database files,
and the raw API pulls behind them) should move to Supabase so the Windows machine can reach them
and they are backed up in the cloud. This handoff records the decision and the checklist. **Nothing
below has been executed.** It was written from a cloud session that could see only the thin `DEV`
router repo, not the project repos, so every project-specific item must be re-verified on a machine
that has the repos on disk.

## Decision

- **No Supabase.** The files are DuckDB; Supabase is Postgres. Moving them means migrating every
  table, rewriting every pipeline to talk to Postgres over the network, and paying latency on every
  query. The two Supabase projects that already exist (`vald-explorer`, `bookvault`) are both paused
  as INACTIVE, which is what the free tier does after a week idle. That is a preview of how a pipeline
  run a few times a week would go.
- **Raw pulls are the source of truth, not the `.duckdb` files.** Pulls land on the primary storage
  drive (Google Drive) as Parquet or CSV, date-partitioned. Each machine rebuilds its own local
  `.duckdb` from them. The `.duckdb` file is a build artifact and never syncs.
- **DuckDB never opens a file that sits in a Drive-synced folder.** DuckDB and SQLite write in place
  and hold locks. Drive copying a file mid-write corrupts it or spawns "conflicted copy" duplicates.
- **Backup is Drive versioning** (30 days of file versions) plus the existing `dailybackup` Drive
  tier. No new backup system.
- **MotherDuck, not Supabase, if a hosted database is ever wanted.** It is DuckDB in the cloud
  (`ATTACH 'md:'`), no schema migration, no pipeline rewrite. External service, so only for datasets
  with no athlete-identifiable data. Not needed for the two-machine problem.
- **Supabase earns its place only for serving**: a Streamlit dashboard or coach PWA that must read
  live data from a server, or concurrent access by other staff. Separate decision.

## What is wrong with the current setup

1. **Windows live-syncs DuckDB files through Google Drive.** Drive for Desktop backs up all of
   `Desktop\DEV` on Windows. The 09-22 handoff already names the long-term fix as not done: move
   non-regenerable data to `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive` and stop backing up DEV. Any
   `.duckdb` or `.db` a pipeline writes inside DEV on Windows is being copied while it is open.
   The Mac side is safer (the `dailybackup` launchd job is an rsync on a schedule) but can still
   catch a file mid-write.
2. **No cross-machine data root.** Both machines already have a `_DRIVE` link inside DEV pointing at
   the primary storage drive (Mac `~/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-eric.rash11@gmail.com/My Drive/00_Primary_Storage_Drive`,
   Windows `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive`). DexaProject, CATES data, and the PP_Recruiting
   outputs already use it. What is missing is a data tier under it and pipelines that read and write

# Unattended follow-up to a scheduled reindex + recall eval (Task Scheduler, \Eric\memsearch-drain-*).
# Runs as the last action of the task, after memsearch-drain.ps1 and recall-eval.py:
#   1. checks the index finished (memsearch-drain.log ends in exit=0),
#   2. checks recall-eval wrote ledger rows in the last 24 h,
#   3. commits + pushes the ledger and results in ~/.claude (nothing else on Windows does),
#   4. writes LATEST.md here with the rows,
#   5. ONLY on a problem, appends one line to .errors.log, which every session surfaces
#      at startup (same pattern as claude-stack-doctor/weekly-check.ps1).
param([string]$Label = '', [switch]$Test)   # -Test: no git, no .errors.log

$ErrorActionPreference = 'Continue'
$here = $PSScriptRoot
$claude = Join-Path $HOME '.claude'
$errLog = Join-Path $claude 'global-memory\transcripts\.errors.log'
$problems = [System.Collections.Generic.List[string]]::new()

$drainLog = Join-Path $claude 'scripts\logs\memsearch-drain.log'
$drainLast = if (Test-Path $drainLog) { Get-Content $drainLog -Tail 1 } else { '' }
$indexOk = $drainLast -match 'exit=0'
if (-not $indexOk) { $problems.Add("index did not finish cleanly (last drain line: '$drainLast')") }

$ledger = Join-Path $here 'ledger.md'
$since = (Get-Date).AddHours(-24).ToString('yyyy-MM-dd')
$rows = @()
if (Test-Path $ledger) {
    $rows = @(Get-Content $ledger | Where-Object { $_ -match '^\| (\d{4}-\d\d-\d\d) ' -and $Matches[1] -ge $since -and (-not $Label -or $_ -match [regex]::Escape("| $Label"))})
}
if ($rows.Count -eq 0) { $problems.Add("recall-eval wrote no ledger rows$(if ($Label) { " labelled '$Label'" }) in the last 24 h") }

$git = 'C:\Program Files\Git\cmd\git.exe'
$pushed = $false
if ($rows.Count -gt 0 -and -not $Test) {
    & $git -C $claude add -- audits/recall-eval/ledger.md audits/recall-eval/results 2>&1 | Out-Null
    & $git -C $claude diff --cached --quiet -- audits/recall-eval
    if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) {
        & $git -C $claude commit -q -m "recall-eval: scheduled run $(Get-Date -Format yyyy-MM-dd) $Label" -- audits/recall-eval/ledger.md audits/recall-eval/results 2>&1 | Out-Null
        & $git -C $claude pull -q --no-rebase --no-edit 2>&1 | Out-Null
        & $git -C $claude push -q 2>&1 | Out-Null
        $pushed = $LASTEXITCODE -eq 0
        if (-not $pushed) { $problems.Add('commit made but git push failed (run git pull/push in ~/.claude)') }
    } else { $pushed = $true }
}

$status = if ($problems.Count) { 'PROBLEM: ' + ($problems -join '; ') } else { 'OK' }
@(
    "# Latest scheduled recall eval"
    ""
    "Run finished $(Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm') on $env:COMPUTERNAME. Status: $status"
    "Index: $drainLast"
    ""
    "| date | machine | label | backend | n | hit@1 | hit@5 | MRR | p50 ms | p95 ms | fail% | coverage% | by layer (hit@5) |"
    "|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|"
) + $rows | Set-Content -LiteralPath (Join-Path $here 'LATEST.md') -Encoding utf8

if ($problems.Count -and -not $Test) {
    Add-Content -LiteralPath $errLog -Encoding utf8 -Value "[$(Get-Date -Format o)] recall-eval scheduled run: $($problems -join '; ') - see ~/.claude/audits/recall-eval/LATEST.md"
}
exit 0
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Recall eval: can each retrieval backend find the known answer file?

Runs every case in questions.jsonl against up to four backends over the SAME
roots (KeystoneOS data/memory-index-paths.json, tokens resolved per machine):

  memsearch  vector search (Milvus + ONNX embedder), top 5 distinct files
  fts5       stdlib SQLite FTS5 / BM25 over whole files, natural-language query
  rg         ripgrep on the case's `keyword`, files ranked by match count
  jev        fts5 top 30, then TypeSafe Jev re-sorts the ALLOWED notes by a yes/no
             "does this note answer the question?" (cloud call; see JEV_ALLOWED)

Per case: rank of the first expected file, latency, failure, and coverage
(does an expected file exist under the configured roots on THIS machine --
the check that exposes path drift like the 2026-09-30 {VAULT} bug).

Writes results/<date>-<machine>-<label>.json and appends one row per backend
to ledger.md. Stdlib only. Spec: ../2026-09-30-memory-infra-audit.md section 6.

  python recall-eval.py --label opus-5.5            # all backends
  python recall-eval.py --backends fts5,rg          # skip memsearch (no Docker / low RAM)
  python recall-eval.py --backends fts5,jev         # needs TYPESAFE_API_KEY or ~/.claude/typesafe.env
"""
import argparse, datetime, json, os, platform, re, shutil, sqlite3, statistics, subprocess, sys, time
import urllib.error, urllib.request
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from pathlib import Path

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
HOME = Path.home()


def first_dir(cands, marker=None):
    for c in cands:
        if (c / marker if marker else c).is_dir():
            return c
    return cands[0]


DEV = first_dir([HOME / "DEV", HOME / "Desktop" / "DEV"], "KeystoneOS")

# Scheduled-task wrapper for recall-eval.py (\Eric\memsearch-drain-*, action 2).
# Task Scheduler discards a direct python action's output, so a failure left no trace
# (2026-10-01: died in ~7 s, ran fine by hand). This keeps stdout+stderr, the exit code,
# and the interpreter context in logs/<date>-<label>.log, and writes logs/last-<label>.txt
# so after-run.ps1 can quote the failure.
param([string]$Label = 'weekly', [string]$Backends = 'memsearch,fts5,rg,jev')

$ErrorActionPreference = 'Continue'
$here = $PSScriptRoot
$logDir = Join-Path $here 'logs'
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $logDir | Out-Null
$log = Join-Path $logDir "$(Get-Date -Format yyyy-MM-dd_HHmm)-$Label.log"
$py = Join-Path $env:LOCALAPPDATA 'Python\bin\python.exe'

function Log([string]$s) { Add-Content -LiteralPath $log -Encoding utf8 -Value $s }

Log "[$(Get-Date -Format o)] start label=$Label backends=$Backends user=$env:USERNAME host=$env:COMPUTERNAME"
Log "python=$py exists=$(Test-Path $py) cwd=$here"
Log "PYTHONIOENCODING=$env:PYTHONIOENCODING PATH=$env:PATH"
try { Log ("python -VV: " + ((& $py -VV 2>&1) -join ' ')) } catch { Log "python -VV threw: $_" }

$env:PYTHONIOENCODING = 'utf-8'
$env:PYTHONUNBUFFERED = '1'
$sw = [Diagnostics.Stopwatch]::StartNew()
try {
    Push-Location $here
    & $py (Join-Path $here 'recall-eval.py') --backends $Backends --label $Label *>&1 |
        ForEach-Object { Log "$_" }
    $code = $LASTEXITCODE
} catch {
    Log "launch threw: $_"
    $code = -1
} finally { Pop-Location }
$sw.Stop()
Log "[$(Get-Date -Format o)] exit=$code elapsed=$([int]$sw.Elapsed.TotalSeconds)s"

$tail = (Get-Content -LiteralPath $log -Tail 4) -join ' / '
"exit=$code log=$log :: $tail" | Set-Content -LiteralPath (Join-Path $logDir "last-$Label.txt") -Encoding utf8

# Keep the newest 20 logs.
Get-ChildItem $logDir -Filter '*.log' | Sort-Object LastWriteTime -Descending |
    Select-Object -Skip 20 | Remove-Item -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
exit $code

toolUseResult.originalFile:
# Unattended follow-up to a scheduled reindex + recall eval (Task Scheduler, \Eric\memsearch-drain-*).
# Runs as the last action of the task, after memsearch-drain.ps1 and recall-eval.py:
#   1. checks the index finished (memsearch-drain.log ends in exit=0),
#   2. checks recall-eval wrote ledger rows in the last 24 h,
#   3. commits + pushes the ledger and results in ~/.claude (nothing else on Windows does),
#   4. writes LATEST.md here with the rows,
#   5. ONLY on a problem, appends one line to .errors.log, which every session surfaces
#      at startup (same pattern as claude-stack-doctor/weekly-check.ps1).
param([string]$Label = '', [switch]$Test)   # -Test: no git, no .errors.log

$ErrorActionPreference = 'Continue'
$here = $PSScriptRoot
$claude = Join-Path $HOME '.claude'
$errLog = Join-Path $claude 'global-memory\transcripts\.errors.log'
$problems = [System.Collections.Generic.List[string]]::new()

$drainLog = Join-Path $claude 'scripts\logs\memsearch-drain.log'
$drainLast = if (Test-Path $drainLog) { Get-Content $drainLog -Tail 1 } else { '' }
$indexOk = $drainLast -match 'exit=0'
if (-not $indexOk) { $problems.Add("index did not finish cleanly (last drain line: '$drainLast')") }

$ledger = Join-Path $here 'ledger.md'
$since = (Get-Date).AddHours(-24).ToString('yyyy-MM-dd')
$rows = @()
if (Test-Path $ledger) {
    $rows = @(Get-Content $ledger | Where-Object { $_ -match '^\| (\d{4}-\d\d-\d\d) ' -and $Matches[1] -ge $since -and (-not $Label -or $_ -match [regex]::Escape("| $Label"))})
}
if ($rows.Count -eq 0) { $problems.Add("recall-eval wrote no ledger rows$(if ($Label) { " labelled '$Label'" }) in the last 24 h") }

$git = 'C:\Program Files\Git\cmd\git.exe'
$pushed = $false
if ($rows.Count -gt 0 -and -not $Test) {
    & $git -C $claude add -- audits/recall-eval/ledger.md audits/recall-eval/results 2>&1 | Out-Null
    & $git -C $claude diff --cached --quiet -- audits/recall-eval
    if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) {
        & $git -C $claude commit -q -m "recall-eval: scheduled run $(Get-Date -Format yyyy-MM-dd) $Label" -- audits/recall-eval/ledger.md audits/recall-eval/results 2>&1 | Out-Null
        & $git -C $claude pull -q --no-rebase --no-edit 2>&1 | Out-Null
        & $git -C $claude push -q 2>&1 | Out-Null
        $pushed = $LASTEXITCODE -eq 0
        if (-not $pushed) { $problems.Add('commit made but git push failed (run git pull/push in ~/.claude)') }
    } else { $pushed = $true }
}

$status = if ($problems.Count) { 'PROBLEM: ' + ($problems -join '; ') } else { 'OK' }
@(
    "# Latest scheduled recall eval"
    ""
    "Run finished $(Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm') on $env:COMPUTERNAME. Status: $status"
    "Index: $drainLast"
    ""
    "| date | machine | label | backend | n | hit@1 | hit@5 | MRR | p50 ms | p95 ms | fail% | coverage% | by layer (hit@5) |"
    "|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|"
) + $rows | Set-Content -LiteralPath (Join-Path $here 'LATEST.md') -Encoding utf8

if ($problems.Count -and -not $Test) {
    Add-Content -LiteralPath $errLog -Encoding utf8 -Value "[$(Get-Date -Format o)] recall-eval scheduled run: $($problems -join '; ') - see ~/.claude/audits/recall-eval/LATEST.md"
}
exit 0

content.text:
Sunday's 02:00 recall eval will now save its output, so if it fails again the cause gets recorded instead of lost.

**What changed**
- **New wrapper `~/.claude/audits/recall-eval/run-eval.ps1`.** Task Scheduler had been throwing away everything the eval printed, so the 10/1 failure left nothing to read. The eval now runs inside this wrapper, which saves its output and errors, the exit code, and which Python and PATH it used to `audits/recall-eval/logs/<date>-<label>.log`. It also writes a one-line `last-<label>.txt`. These logs are kept out of git.
- **`after-run.ps1` now explains failures.** When the eval writes no ledger rows, the error line it adds to `.errors.log` includes that one-line summary, so the next session start shows why it failed.
- **Both scheduled tasks now call the wrapper for the eval step** (`\Eric\memsearch-drain-weekly` and `-once`). The weekly task's next run is still Sun 10/4 02:00.

**Checked:** I ran the wrapper once through Task Scheduler with the fast fts5 search only. It exited cleanly, the log held the full output, and it scored the same 25/30 as before. I removed the test task and its ledger row and result files afterwards. Both repos are pushed (`~/.claude` and DEV `c9520fa`).

**The original failure didn't come back** in that test, so I still don't know what caused it. Since fts5 alone ran fine, my guess is the memsearch or Jev search after the 4-hour reindex. I didn't test those two here because a memsearch run is slow and Jev calls cost money. Sunday's full run will show which it is.

**Next:** Sunday or Monday, check `LATEST.md`. If it says PROBLEM, read the newest `logs/*-weekly.log`. That's noted in DEV `STATUS.md`.

Source: YouTube channel @42analytics (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference talks, 2012-2026). Text corpus built in `DEV/42Analytics` (private repo `erash11/42Analytics`); this note records what is staged for Flint.

## What is staged

- `staging/sources/42analytics/<folder>/` (local only, gitignored): `transcript.md` (auto-captions, 30 s timestamp markers), `summary.md`, `applications.md`, `meta.json`. 128 talks. `staging/sources/42analytics/manifest.tsv` lists id, date, title, event, topics, confidence, URL.
- Atomized 2026-10-01: the 23 `supported` talks became 152 entries in `staging/library/sports-analytics-and-decision-making/ssac-talks--42analytics/` (26 supported, 119 untested, 7 contested). Independent Opus review of a 50-entry sample (14 GO, 36 FIX, 0 NO-GO) found confidence set too high, Q&A attributions beyond the captions, smoothed garbles and dropped baseline tags; all fixed, plus a pattern sweep of the other 102. Reports: `staging/review_42analytics_r0.md` to `r3.md`. Not promoted: a second independent review round is still needed. Not in the vault.
- Regenerate the staged copy from the repo: copy each `42Analytics/videos/<folder>/` (use `baylor_application.md` as `applications.md` in the pilot folder `2025-03-18...7G9AKDKHVlA` if present).

## Quality state (read before atomizing)

- Summaries were mechanically checked (time locators inside transcript range and near a marker; numbers present in caption text) and a 15-video Opus adversarial pass found about 45 defects, all fixed. The other 113 got the mechanical check and the baseline-line check only.
- Confidence: 23 `supported` (talks that show a method plus results), 104 `untested` (vendor pitches, panels without data, single cases, book promotions, policy talks), 1 pilot summary without frontmatter tag.
- Captions are auto-generated: names and numbers are often garbled and speakers are unlabeled. Treat attributions to named people as unverified unless the speaker states them aloud.
- `applications.md` follows the voice rules: "Eric's baseline:" lines were checked against `docs/method-baseline.md` (82 fixes, mostly missing Inferred tags). Baseline lines tagged Inferred carry the course-team, speaker-unconfirmed caveat. `method-baseline.md` contradicts itself on speed re-exposure (line ~99 vs ~150); resolve before relying on it.
- Not covered: 6 tier A talks not yet fetched (YouTube rate limit) and 5 with no captions; tier B (about 117 lower-priority talks) not started.

## Atomization plan (first pass done; promotion pending)

1. Start with the 23 `supported` talks (list below); entries cite `summary.md` and transcript locators, with the talk as the author voice and `untested` for anything the speaker only asserts.
2. Follow `docs/ATOMIZE_BRIEF.md` and the ingest review gate (independent reviewer before promotion).
3. Dedup against the vault library before each entry; `untested` talks mostly add Related links or case-studies rather than principles.

    python scripts/promote_to_vault.py <domain>/<book> [...]            # dry run
    python scripts/promote_to_vault.py <domain>/<book> [...] --apply    # copy

vault (never deleted), and every [[link]] in the promoted files that would not resolve
against the vault as it will be after promotion. _domain.md files are never copied over an
existing vault file (merge those by hand); a domain new to the vault gets its staged
_domain.md. Nothing is committed: commit in the vault afterwards.
After promotion the vault copy is canonical (reciprocal links are added there), so sync the
book back into staging. For a book already in the vault, a "changed" file you did not edit in
staging means investigate, not copy: --apply overwrites the vault file.
"""

import filecmp
import re
import shutil
import sys
from pathlib import Path

VAULT = Path(r"C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library")
LINK = re.compile(r"\[\[([^\]|#\n]+)")
def names(p: Path, root: Path) -> set[str]:
    rel = p.relative_to(root).with_suffix("").as_posix()
    return {p.stem, rel, f"{p.parent.name}/{p.stem}"}
def main() -> int:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("books", nargs="+", help="<domain>/<book> under staging/library")
    ap.add_argument("--apply", action="store_true")
    a = ap.parse_args()
    known: set[str] = set()
    for p in VAULT.rglob("*.md"):
        known |= names(p, VAULT)
    plan = []
    for book in a.books:
        src = STAGING / book
        if not src.is_dir():
            print(f"missing staging folder: {src}")
            return 2
        for p in src.glob("*.md"):
            known |= names(p, STAGING)
        plan.append((book, src, VAULT / book))
    unresolved = 0
    for book, src, dst in plan:
        new = [p.name for p in src.glob("*.md") if not (dst / p.name).exists()]
        changed = [p.name for p in src.glob("*.md")
                   if (dst / p.name).exists() and not filecmp.cmp(p, dst / p.name, shallow=False)]
        vault_only = sorted(p.name for p in dst.glob("*.md") if not (src / p.name).exists()) if dst.exists() else []
        print(f"\n== {book}: {len(new)} new, {len(changed)} changed, {len(vault_only)} vault-only")
        for n in changed:

`fixes_supertraining_ch4-2b_applied.md`, `review_supertraining_ch4-2b_opus_round2.md` and
`fixes_supertraining_ch4-1_applied.md`. Every pair below was checked against the actual
current file content: source and target both confirmed to exist (in the vault library or in
one of the three staged folders promoted in this wave), each Source resolves to exactly one
file by `<book>/<file>.md` suffix once those folders are promoted, and the source file (vault
copy and, where one exists, staging copy) was scanned for an existing `[[...target-slug...]]`
def add(text: str, line: str) -> str:
    lines = text.rstrip("\n").split("\n")
    if "## Related knowledge" in text:
        i = next(k for k, l in enumerate(lines) if l.startswith("## Related knowledge"))
        j = i + 1
        while j < len(lines) and not lines[j].startswith("## "):
            j += 1
        block = [l for l in lines[i + 1:j] if l.strip() and "None identified" not in l]
        if block and not block[-1].startswith("- "):
            block.append("")
        return "\n".join(lines[:i + 1] + [""] + block + [f"- {line}", ""] + lines[j:]).rstrip("\n") + "\n"
    rel = [k for k, l in enumerate(lines) if l.startswith("**Related**")]
    if rel:
        j = rel[-1] + 1
        while j < len(lines) and lines[j].strip() and not lines[j].startswith("**"):
            j += 1
        lines[j - 1] = lines[j - 1].rstrip().rstrip(".;") + "; " + line
        return "\n".join(lines) + "\n"
    return "\n".join(lines + ["", f"**Related** — {line}"]) + "\n"
def main() -> int:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("table")
    ap.add_argument("--apply", action="store_true")
    a = ap.parse_args()
    rows = [r for r in Path(a.table).read_text(encoding="utf-8").split("\n## Dropped")[0].splitlines()
            if r.startswith("| ") and "[[" in r]
    done = skipped = failed = 0
    for r in rows:
        cells = [c.strip() for c in r.strip().strip("|").split("|")]
        src, target, text = cells[0], cells[1], cells[3]
        slug = re.search(r"\[\[([^\]|]+)", target).group(1).split("/")[-1]
        path = resolve(src)
        if path is None:
            failed += 1
            print(f"UNRESOLVED source: {src}")
            continue
        body = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        if re.search(r"\[\[[^\]]*" + re.escape(slug) + r"[\]|#]", body):
            skipped += 1
            continue
        done += 1
        print(f"{'ADD' if a.apply else 'would add'}: {path.relative_to(VAULT).as_posix()} -> {slug}")
        if a.apply:
            path.write_text(add(body, text), encoding="utf-8")
    print(f"\n{done} {'added' if a.apply else 'to add'}, {skipped} already linked, {failed} unresolved")

-# Decision Gates: Five Elements That Turn Data Into a Decision

-**What it is** — A decision gate is "a predefined checkpoint in your workflow where you review agreed criteria and make a clear call before progressing: Go / Modify / Stop" (Lab_2D_Decision_Gates.pdf p.1). Weber's five required elements: **(1) what's being evaluated**: named specifically enough to build criteria around (not "hamstring injury" but "eccentric knee flexor strength" or "sprint exposure tolerance, defined speed band and volume"); **(2) criteria**: pass (green, proceed), fail (red, stop/regress), and borderline (amber, confirm/repeat/add a data point), plus an explicit definition of what counts as a breach; **(3) decision options**: progress, hold, regress, refer, escalate, matched to the sport's and medical setup's actual resources; **(4) ownership**: who provides inputs, who interprets results, and who owns the final call, since "if ownership is unclear, gates become meetings instead of decisions"; **(5) next step**: the immediate action a pass, fail, or borderline result triggers, including a re-test or review timeframe (pp.1–2). Weber also insists gates carry logistics-realistic timeframes stated in advance ("First clinical review happens within X hours," "Imaging is expected within Y days if criteria are met") so a department is not improvising timelines after an injury occurs (p.2).

-**Why it works** — Weber's own stated mechanism: when staff send raw reports to coaches and senior medical staff without a pre-agreed structure, "people interpret numbers differently, and emotion enters the room, especially around selection" (p.2). **Inference:** agreeing the five elements before the pressure of an actual decision arrives removes the negotiation from the moment it is least likely to go well.

-**When to apply** — Any recurring return-to-play, load-progression, or technology-adoption decision that currently gets re-litigated case by case. **Eric's baseline:** "KPI-threshold identification for diagnostic screening and performance testing" is named as a departmental operating principle, but "no specific RTP criteria, battery, or phased-return protocol appears anywhere in this corpus" [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play]. **Inference:** this framework is a direct template for building that missing protocol, element by element.

-**When NOT to apply** — A decision gate is indefensible without knowing how noisy the underlying measurement is; Weber's own next lab makes this explicit: see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for the statistics a gate's criteria depend on. This framework also assumes a genuine, pre-identifiable decision point exists; it is not suited to open-ended diagnostic or brainstorming work (see [[framework--meeting-typology-decide-diagnose-inform-build]] for when "decide" is the wrong mode to reach for).

-**Example** — Weber's own lab task: build one performance gate (e.g., speed-exposure progression) and one rehab gate (e.g., hamstring return-to-run), each specifying key quality, pass/fail/borderline criteria, decision options, ownership, and next step plus timeframe (p.3).

-**Related** — [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]]: the statistical foundation a gate's criteria need. [[framework--monitoring-versus-testing]]: where the "if this result, then this action" decision matrix first appears. [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]]: the record-keeping companion to a gate's decision; [[research-papers/robertson-2017-red-amber-or-green-athlete-monitoring-in-team-sport-the-need-for-decision-support-systems]]: peer-reviewed red/amber/green decision-support framework matching this course's five-element gate; [[rehab-and-return-to-play/on-field-rtp--harries/heuristic--75-85-percent-mv-decision-gate]]: a concrete, sport-specific worked example of a five-element-style decision gate

-# The Decision Log: Action, Owner, Due Date, Review

-**What it is** — A minimal written record Weber attaches to the end of every decision-oriented meeting format in the course: the action taken, who owns it, the due date, and the review method and date (Lab 3A summary (Kaigi-summary.md), 04:48–05:56). The same four fields recur, worded slightly differently, in every later meeting format, per the lesson summaries: the meeting-typology **decide** mode requires an explicit decision, owner, due date, and review (Lab 3B summary, 01:03–02:14); stoplight storytelling ends with one owner, one action, a due date, and a review point recorded in the decision log (Lab 3C summary, 03:02–03:45); and the 20-minutes-of-discipline format ends with the decision, actions, accountable people, deadlines, and a requested update (Podcast 3 summary, 08:34–09:39).

-**Why it works** — Weber's stated rationale, per the lesson summary, is that the administrative effort of writing the four fields down creates accountability and reduces later disagreement about what was agreed (Lab 3A summary (Kaigi-summary.md), 04:48–05:56). **Inference:** without a record, a verbal decision is likely subject to selective memory once circumstances change or the outcome is unwelcome; the log exists specifically to prevent that after-the-fact renegotiation.

-**When to apply** — The closing step of any decision meeting, regardless of which format (kaigi, stoplight, a 20-minute recurring meeting, or an informal hallway decision that is being made official). **Eric's baseline:** no specific RTP criteria, battery, or phased-return protocol appears anywhere in the reviewed corpus, even though KPI-threshold identification is named as a departmental operating principle [method-baseline.md, Rehab and return to play]. **Inference:** a decision log does not supply the missing criteria, but it does supply the accountability structure once a criterion-based decision is made.

-**When NOT to apply** — This is a record-keeping minimum, not a full decision framework by itself; it assumes a decision has already been reached through some other structure (a kaigi meeting, a decision gate) and simply captures it. It also does not specify where the log should live or how it should be reviewed at scale; Weber's course gives the four fields, not a system for storing or auditing them over a season.

-**Example** — Weber's stoplight-storytelling version adds one more requirement to the same four fields, per the lesson summary: every status, including amber, needs a next action or review date (Lab 3C summary, 05:51–06:23). **Inference:** this closes the loophole of an ambiguous "wait and see" outcome with no owner attached.

-**Related** — [[framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure]]: where this log format originates in the course. -# Evidence Stacking: Don't Decide on One Dramatic Signal

-**What it is** — Weber's central question for any consequential decision, per the lesson summary: does staff have enough independent, relevant information to act (Podcast 2 summary, 00:00–02:20). A dramatic single result or first impression should prompt further investigation, not settle the decision. An evidence stack combines the event/problem history, clinical findings where relevant, the athlete's own prior results, movement and capacity checks, and performance under the conditions the decision actually concerns (00:00–02:20). His practical takeaway: define the decision first, identify the important unanswered questions, then choose measures that each add distinct evidence rather than repeating what is already known (17:35–18:15). This is the same caution Weber repeats in narrower form elsewhere in the course: in Lab 2A, one test returning to baseline is treated as one data point rather than a stand-alone clearance (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02); in Webinar 1 Part III, one favorable test result is not a complete return-to-running answer (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 07:44–08:54); and in Podcast 1, he warns specifically against treating a single red dashboard indicator as automatic grounds to remove an athlete (Podcast 1 summary, 03:38–04:24).

-**Why it works** — Weber's own stated purpose, per the lesson summary, is to separate meaningful change from noise and to communicate decisions with appropriate confidence (Podcast 2 summary, 00:00–02:20). **Inference:** the likely reason combining sources helps is that different evidence types fail in different, largely independent ways: a single clinical impression, a single hop-test result, and a single speed-exposure metric can each individually mislead, but they are unlikely to all mislead in the same direction at once. Updating the working assessment as each new piece arrives, illustrated with Weber's soccer-knee and hamstring anecdotes (02:20–17:35), is more robust than treating any one piece as decisive.

-**When to apply** — Any return-to-play, load, or selection decision where one metric alone is being used to justify the call, especially under time pressure or when a result is unusually dramatic (very good or very bad). **Eric's baseline:** the course transcripts in Eric's own corpus argue "you don't need a fancy test or anything to do that. But you do have to have a good coach's eye," while Eric's own SportSmith writing moved the opposite direction on daily monitoring by replacing subjective wellness surveys with objective mRSI [method-baseline.md Tensions #3]. **Inference:** evidence stacking offers a synthesis rather than forcing a choice between those two positions: the coach's eye is one more independent stream to stack alongside the objective metric, not a competitor to it.

-**When NOT to apply** — Per the lesson summary's own caveat (not Weber's words), the anecdotes illustrate a reasoning approach and do not establish that a triple-hop baseline can diagnose a knee injury; medical diagnosis and clearance remain clinical decisions (Podcast 2 summary, practical takeaway). It also does not specify how many independent streams are enough for a given decision; that judgment is left to the practitioner.

-**Example** — Weber's hamstring case: clinical progress and gym measures were supplemented with hopping, running-speed exposure, and a comparison of running mechanics at matched speeds, specifically to close the gap between controlled tests and actual field demands before returning the athlete to competition (Podcast 2 summary, 10:30–17:35). The reported outcome is one case, not a validated return-to-play rule. Untested anecdote (n=1). The mechanics comparison used SpeedSig, Weber's own product (Podcast 2 transcript 00:15:52 to 00:16:18); treat the case as an illustration by an interested party, not evidence for the product or the return pathway.

-**Related** — [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]]: the single-measurement discipline this framework scales up. [[framework--decision-gate-five-elements]]: where a completed evidence stack feeds a formal go/hold/stop decision. [[principle--protocol-drift-undermines-comparability]]: the reliability discipline each stream in the stack still needs individually.

-# The Knowledge x Behaviour Matrix

-**What it is** — A 2x2 grid Weber uses to discuss staff capability separately from staff engagement. The **knowledge axis** (horizontal): **handbrake** (insufficient or poorly aligned knowledge for the setting), **pawn** (fundamentals without complex problem-solving), **practitioner** (strong across domains, able to contribute), **operator** (broad knowledge, independent complex problem-solving) (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 07:35–10:00). The **behaviour axis** (vertical): **misaligned**, **coasting** (contributes in a stable role without pushing change), **catalyst** (proactively influences the team even without leading change alone), and **beacon** at the top of the range (Webinar 1 Part II summary, 10:00–11:57; Lab 1B Part 2 summary, 00:00–01:07). Weber is explicit these are role-capability labels, meant to describe knowledge and behaviour rather than to judge a person's overall worth (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 03:59–06:10). A companion student worksheet (published under Weber's SpeedSig brand) operationalizes the grid as a self-audit: define both axes in your own words, self-place on each axis now and for a 3–5 year target, then map 3–5 colleagues onto the same categories using initials or role titles only (Knowledge_Behaviour_Profile_Student_Workbook.pdf, Sections A–C). The behaviour axis has four levels in the video (Webinar 1 Part II transcript 00:10:21 to 00:12:16: misaligned, coasting, catalyst, beacon) and in the Grey Zone Workbook p.2, but three in the Lab 1b blog and the student workbook (A3). Beacon is the top tier; the three-level handouts omit it.

-**Why it works** — Weber gives the grid two uses: development (spot skill gaps, plan CPD: Lab 1B Part 2 summary 02:10 to 04:04) and selection (Lab 1B Part 1 transcript 00:07:40 to 00:08:02: misaligned staff "need to be managed out"; Lab_1b blog p.4: "Make tough calls on the misaligned"). **Inference:** splitting knowledge from behaviour also separates two different interventions, a low-knowledge/high-catalyst person likely needs training, while a high-knowledge/coasting person needs a different kind of push, consistent with Weber's own worked contrast (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 00:00–03:27).

-**When to apply** — Structuring a 1:1 development conversation, a hiring discussion, or a mentoring assignment where the real question is whether a person needs more knowledge, more engagement, or both. Weber's advice to pick a mentor above you who has worked in elite sport (Lab 1B Part 1 transcript, 06:10–07:07) is a direct extension of the knowledge axis; see [[heuristic--choose-a-mentor-above-you-who-has-worked-in-elite-sport]].

-**When NOT to apply** — Do not use this grid, or any output from the SpeedSig worksheet, to place a named Baylor colleague into a "handbrake" or "misaligned" category in any written record; Weber's own framing is explicit that the grid is meant to evaluate knowledge and behavior, not a person's overall worth (Lab 1B Part 1 summary, 03:59–06:10), and the course's own worksheet instructs anonymizing colleagues by role title for exactly this reason. It is also entirely self- or supervisor-report, with no validation evidence that placement on the grid predicts performance or that movement between quadrants is trainable on any particular timeline. Inference: any real personnel decision would still need direct evidence, fair process and Baylor HR policy (the lesson summary adds the same caveat).

-**Example** — Weber's own worked contrast: someone with limited knowledge but strong initiative may be worth developing, while deep expertise paired with little engagement can hold a team's progress back (Webinar 1 Part III summary, 00:00–03:27).

-**Related** — [[heuristic--make-development-visible-with-cpd-checkins]] and [[heuristic--choose-a-mentor-above-you-who-has-worked-in-elite-sport]]: the two concrete practices Weber pairs with this matrix.

-# Measurement vs. Inference

-**What it is** — Weber's distinction between what a tool actually captures (a **measurement**: force, distance, speed, displacement) and the explanation applied to that output (an **inference**: fatigue, tissue status, readiness) (Lab 2A summary, 00:00–01:45). His examples, per the lesson summary: calling a lower countermovement-jump result neurological fatigue, or a GPS change tissue stress: neither label follows directly from the measurement alone, and athletes can produce a similar output through a different movement strategy, so a stable score can hide a real change in mechanics (01:45–03:20). His stated communication rule: report what was measured, identify what is being inferred, state your confidence in that inference, and recommend the next exposure or check (05:02–06:02).

-**Why it works** — Weber's stated reasons: overstating certainty "is what drives coaches crazy" (Lab_2a PDF p.2; transcript 00:02:09 to 00:02:17), and because "humans are an incredibly redundant system" the same output can hide different strategies (Lab_2a PDF p.2), so an inference has to be built by triangulation to a probability, not asserted (PDF p.3; transcript 00:03:20 to 00:04:01). **Inference:** collapsing the distinction likely lets a causal story ride along silently with a number, so the story gets treated with the same confidence as the measurement itself. Naming the inference as an inference forces an explicit confidence statement instead of an implicit one, and makes the underlying reasoning available for someone else to challenge.

-**When to apply** — Any report or conversation where a device output is being used to say something about the athlete's internal state (fatigue, readiness, tissue tolerance) rather than just the output itself. **Eric's baseline:** modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were" [method-baseline.md, Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring]. **Inference:** this framework's discipline would ask the same question of mRSI that Weber asks of his CMJ example, what is actually measured (jump-derived force/time output), and what is being inferred from it (neuromuscular readiness), stated with what confidence.

-**When NOT to apply** — This is a communication and reasoning discipline, not a claim that inference is unreliable or should be avoided; Weber's own examples (hamstring context: injury history, strength tests, jumping/hopping, speed exposure, running mechanics) show that combining several measurements to support one inference is the intended use, not a replacement for inference altogether (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02). It also does not by itself tell you whether an observed change exceeds measurement noise: see [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]] for that separate question.

-**Example** — Weber treats one test returning to baseline as one data point, not a stand-alone clearance, in his hamstring illustration (Lab 2A summary, 03:20–05:02), the same discipline generalized into a full framework in [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]].

-**Related** — [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]]: combining multiple inferences before acting on any one of them. [[framework--reliability-vs-sensitivity-mdc-and-swc]]: whether the measurement itself is trustworthy before it is interpreted. [[principle--means-and-modality-before-technology]]: the upstream discipline of naming the question before choosing what to measure.

project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.

- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

# Closeout

One command that replaces the manual end-of-day sequence: "any loose ends?" → "commit and push what needs to be" → "is this in memory?" → "write a handoff so Codex can pick this up."

Run all five checks, then give ONE verdict. Do not ask permission between steps — the invocation of this skill IS the authorization for the full sequence. Commit and push is standing-authorized for every DEV repo: each repo's `AGENTS.md` Session routine says "update STATUS, commit, push at end", and unpushed work on one machine is the top cause of conflicts on the other. The only exceptions are repos whose `CLAUDE.md` says their data must stay local (DexaProject is the precedent); commit those locally and list them as open.

This one file serves Claude Code, Codex and Cowork (uploaded to claude.ai). Cowork has no TaskList and no Claude Code memory hooks: do what applies there and say what was skipped.

## Step 1 — Loose-ends sweep

- `git status` across **every** repo in DEV, not only the ones named in this conversation. Another session, another harness, or the other machine may have left work dirty, and a closeout that only checks what it remembers touching will say "clear to sign off" over someone else's uncommitted work. Walk `DEV/`, `DEV/Football/` and `DEV/SpecialRequests/`, and report any repo with uncommitted or unpushed commits. The full walk takes about 90 seconds.
  - Windows: `git -C <repo> status --porcelain` per repo. Do NOT use `Get-ChildItem -Recurse` to look for files; it silently skips paths past the 260-character limit. Inside a repo, `git ls-files` is the reliable way to ask whether a file exists.
  - Repos with dirty state you did not touch: commit and push them like any other, and name them in the report so the user knows another session left them.
- Unfinished todos/tasks from this session (TaskList if available).
- Background jobs or workflows still running.
- Anything the user was promised earlier in the session that wasn't delivered.

## Step 2 — Commit & push

- Every repo touched this session: stage, commit with a descriptive message, `git pull --no-rebase` (the other machine may have pushed), push. If the merge conflicts, follow the conflict steps in `dev-sync/SKILL.md` (they are the one home for them), then push and list the file under "Still open".
- Before staging, make sure any new file over 95 MB and any `.env` is in `.gitignore`.
- Local-only repos (CLAUDE.md says so): commit, do not push, list it.
- Also check the three config repos, `~/.claude` (dotclaude), `~/.claude/skills` (claude-skills) and `~/.claude/global-memory` (claude-global-memory). If any has changes, commit and push it the same way, so the other machine's `/dev-sync` picks it up.
- **Push `global-memory` even on a light session.** `daily-backup` pushes it nightly, which is too late for a same-day handoff: work the Mac in the afternoon, sit down at Windows that evening, and anything written to MEMORY.md or handoffs is still only on the Mac. Pushing it here is what makes memory available to the other machine tonight rather than tomorrow. It is the only repo that carries memory across, so treat an unpushed `global-memory` the same as an unpushed project repo: it blocks "clear to sign off".
- Nothing to commit → say so in one line, move on.

## Step 3 — Memory verification
